title: Cardiac parasympathetic reactivation following exercise: implications for training prescription
authors: Stanley J, Peake JM, Buchheit M
population: Athletes and healthy individuals after single aerobic exercise sessions (quantitative analysis of published data)
findings: Time required for complete cardiac autonomic recovery after a single aerobic-based session is up to 24 h after low-intensity exercise, 24-48 h after threshold-intensity exercise and at least 48 h after high-intensity exercise.
Based on limited data, exercise duration is unlikely to be the greatest determinant of cardiac parasympathetic reactivation.
Cardiac autonomic recovery occurs more rapidly in individuals with greater aerobic fitness.
Parasympathetic reactivation does not appear to coincide with recovery of all physiological systems (e.g. energy stores or the neuromuscular system).
Coaches should structure programmes tailored to each individual's recovery kinetics; the review gives recommendations for structuring microcycles.
limitations: Narrative review with quantitative pooling of heterogeneous studies; autonomic recovery is one recovery system and may not match muscular, tendon or glycogen recovery; limited data after resistance exercise and none specific to long runs or ultras.
implications: Hard-easy rule: after a high-intensity session allow at least 48 h before the next hard session; after threshold work 24-48 h; easy running needs no spacing. Encode as minimum spacing between quality sessions.

Fitter athletes may use the shorter end of the range (supported by the fitness finding); use 48 h for novices or when readiness is low (design choice). Long runs are not covered, so use a separate conservative rule.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed match (Sports Med 2013;43(12):1259-77). Numbers verified in PubMed abstract.
